HIST 270 · Chapter 5 · Lecture 1

The Sui Tragedy

The Dynasty That Reunited China—and Broke Itself

A tragedy in three acts · 581–618

AI-generated historical interpretation · Dunhuang-inspired mural style

This lecture tells the short history of the Sui dynasty as a tragedy in three acts. The title image is an AI-generated historical interpretation, not a surviving Sui painting. Read it from left to right: imperial power, canal construction and grain transport, and finally the violence that ended the dynasty. Those three zones preview the lecture’s arc.

The Sui ruled from 581 to 618. In that brief span, it ended centuries of political division, created a state powerful enough to move officials, grain, workers, and armies across enormous distances, and then collapsed when that same machinery demanded more than communities could sustain. The tragedy is not that Sui state-building failed. Much of it succeeded so well that the Tang kept it. The tragedy is that the rulers used their new capacity without accepting limits.

Keep one sentence in mind: Wendi built the machine; Yangdi drove it past the breaking point; the Tang inherited what survived.

Check yourself: What are the three stages suggested by the title image?

Cold open · Jiangdu, 618

The emperor who commanded millions could no longer command his own guard.

Rebellions had severed the empire.
Yangdi had withdrawn to Jiangdu.
Officers from his own guard killed him.
Li Yuan already controlled Chang’an.
Thirty-seven years earlier, Yangdi’s father had founded the Sui. The tragedy begins with the question: what broke?

We begin at the end. In spring 618, Emperor Yangdi was at Jiangdu, today’s Yangzhou, while rebellions and rival armies divided the empire. Officers from his own guard, led by men associated with Yuwen Huaji, turned against him and killed him. The AI-generated image imagines the tense final separation between the emperor and the soldiers who were supposed to protect him; it does not claim to reproduce the actual room or exact moment.

Yangdi’s death was not the only ending taking place. Li Yuan had already captured Chang’an in 617 and installed Yangdi’s grandson as a puppet emperor. After news of Yangdi’s death, Li Yuan removed the puppet and founded the Tang. The Sui dynasty disappeared, but its capital, canals, laws, offices, and reunified territory did not.

This is the mystery the lecture must solve: how did the dynasty that reunited China lose the loyalty of farmers, soldiers, officials, governors, and finally its own guard?

Check yourself: Why is Yangdi’s death a political symbol as well as a personal tragedy?

The story we must explain

One dynasty. Three acts. One fatal contradiction.

I

Seizing the Realm

Yang Jian takes a throne, crosses the Yangzi, and reunifies China.

II

Building the Machine

Officials, canals, registers, taxes, soldiers, and religion bind the empire together.

III

Breaking the Empire

Yangdi pushes the machine beyond what households and elites will bear.

The tragedy: successful state-building gave the Sui the power to exhaust the society that sustained it.

This slide is the roadmap for the lecture. Each act begins with a different kind of power.

Act I, Seizing the Realm, follows Yang Jian as he takes the Northern Zhou throne, becomes Emperor Wendi, and conquers the southern Chen. Military victory reunifies China in 589, but conquest does not automatically create loyalty. Act II, Building the Machine, explains how the Sui connected the realm through court appointments, written examinations, canals, household registers, taxation, military service, and Buddhist kingship. These systems made the empire governable. Act III, Breaking the Empire, follows Yangdi as he uses those systems for construction and distant wars until service to the state begins to look like a death sentence.

The final line is the interpretation to test against the evidence: the Sui did not collapse because it was weak. It collapsed because a powerful state repeatedly ignored the human limits beneath its power.

Check yourself: Which act explains Sui success, and which act explains why that success became dangerous?

Act I · 581–590

Seizing the Realm

First the throne. Then the south. Then the harder problem: governing the conquered.

AI-generated historical interpretation · Dunhuang-inspired mural style

Act I begins with a court crisis rather than a battlefield. Yang Jian was already one of the most powerful men in the Northern Zhou state. His daughter had married Emperor Xuan, and when the throne passed to the young Emperor Jing, Yang Jian controlled the government. In 581 he took the throne and founded the Sui. The AI-generated image places the adult statesman and the child emperor at opposite ends of a vast hall to make the imbalance of power visible. It is an interpretation, not a documentary image.

The act’s title, Seizing the Realm, has two meanings. Yang Jian first seized a dynasty from within the northern ruling elite. He then used the armies and resources inherited from Northern Zhou to seize the southern Chen and reunify China. Both achievements depended on coercion, but lasting rule would require more than fear.

Watch for a recurring problem: every victory creates a new governing challenge. Taking the throne requires legitimacy; taking the south requires integration.

Check yourself: What two different “seizures” make up Act I?

Founding the Sui · 581

Yang Jian turned Northern Zhou power into a new dynasty.

Throne seizure

Yang Jian took the throne from his young step-grandson, Emperor Jing, and founded the Sui in 581.

Securing power by force

He killed fifty-nine princes of the Zhou royal house, and later the boy emperor, so the old ruling family could not return to power.

The Sui began through a transfer of power within the northern ruling elite, not through a popular movement.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

This slide shows how the Sui began: not with a popular uprising, but with a powerful insider taking the throne.

Yang Jian was tied to the Northern Zhou royal family through his daughter, Yang Lihua, who was the empress of Emperor Xuan. The child emperor Jing was Xuan’s son by another consort, so he was Yang Jian’s step-grandson, not his blood grandson. In 581, Yang Jian took the throne from him and founded the Sui. He then killed fifty-nine princes of the Zhou royal house, and later the boy emperor himself, so the old ruling family could not come back to power.

Look at the portrait. It comes from the Thirteen Emperors scroll, attributed to the Tang court painter Yan Liben and painted decades after Wendi died. It shows how Tang artists imagined a powerful founding emperor, not what Yang Jian really looked like. Notice how the emperor towers over his attendants.

“Wendi” (“Cultured Emperor”) is a title given after his death. While he ruled, years were counted by his reign names, Kaihuang (581–600) and Renshou (601–604).

Check yourself: Why would Yang Jian kill the Zhou princes, and what does that suggest about how secure a new dynasty felt?

A northern ruling world

The Sui ruling family belonged to an intermarried northwestern elite.

Yang Jian’s family

Yang claimed Han Chinese descent, but his family may have had Xianbei roots.

His wife’s family connected Chinese and non-Chinese lineages.

Why identity is complex

Chinese and Xianbei families intermarried and served across northern regimes.

Family names and political service do not map neatly onto modern ethnic categories.

Xianbei: nomadic peoples from the northern grasslands whose leaders ruled much of north China before the Sui.

The Sui reunified China from a political world already shaped by cultural and ethnic mixing.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

This slide asks a tricky question: who were the Sui rulers, culturally speaking?

Yang Jian claimed descent from Han Chinese ancestors, but his family may have had Xianbei roots. The Xianbei were nomadic peoples from the northern grasslands whose leaders ruled much of north China before the Sui. His wife, Empress Dugu, came from a family with both Chinese and non-Chinese connections, and his daughter married into the Northern Zhou royal family.

Why this matters: after generations of intermarriage and shared government service, the northern ruling class was a mix of Chinese and Xianbei families. You can’t tell someone’s ethnic background simply from a family name or from which dynasty he served, and modern ethnic labels don’t fit this world neatly. So it is misleading to picture the Sui as “Chinese” rulers replacing “foreign” ones. The Sui claimed to restore a Chinese empire, but it grew out of this mixed northern world, and so did the Tang, whose ruling family came from the same elite (slide 24).

Check yourself: Why is it hard to label the Sui ruling family as simply “Chinese” or simply “Xianbei”?

The great obstacle · winter 588–589

Before the Sui could rule the south, it had to cross the Yangzi.

The barrier: Chen rulers relied on the wide river as a defensive wall.
The answer: Sui armies and fleets formed a front from Sichuan to the sea.
The result: Jiankang fell in 589; more than three centuries of division ended.
The river crossing won the war. It did not yet win the south.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

This diagram shows the biggest obstacle to reunification: the Yangzi River. It is a simple sketch, not a scale map. It places the Sui capital, Chang’an, in the northwest and the Chen capital, Jiankang (modern Nanjing), on the far side of the river in the southeast.

The Yangzi is wide, and the southern courts had long used it as a defensive barrier against northern armies, which were strongest on land. To cross it, Sui commanders built a large fleet. By late 588 they had troops lined up along the river from Sichuan to the sea, and in 589 they took Jiankang.

What to notice: the dashed arrow sums up forces moving south; it is not the route of a single army. The real campaign stretched along the whole length of the river.

Why this matters: geography shaped how reunification happened. A northern state could not simply march south; it had to adapt its military power to a river environment. This is the key military step in the conquest part of the lecture.

Check yourself: Why did the Sui need ships, not just land armies, to conquer the south?

The conquest of Chen

The Sui took the south by force, then worked to win it over.

Late 588Sui troops gather along the Yangzi.
589Jiankang falls and is razed; Chen nobles and officials are moved north.
590A large southern revolt is crushed by the general Yang Su.
590sTax relief and mild rule by Prince Yang Guang win southern support.
Political reunification did not mean equal treatment of the conquered south.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

×

Holding the south, 589–600

Revolt (590): In late 590, rumors spread that southerners would be moved north. A revolt began near Lake Tai and spread far to the south. Sui forces under Yang Su put it down.

Tax relief: Wendi freed the former Chen lands from taxes for ten years to help win their loyalty.

A prince in the south: Wendi’s son Yang Guang, the future Emperor Yangdi, governed the south as viceroy from 591 to 600. He was married to a princess from the southern Liang royal family, and his fairly mild rule helped bring southern elites into the Sui empire.

This timeline shows that conquering the south was only half the job; holding it was the other half.

In 589, Jiankang fell. The Sui razed the city and moved Chen nobles and officials north, which broke up the southern political class that might have rebuilt a rival court. In late 590, rumors spread that southerners would be moved north, and a large revolt broke out. The general Yang Su crushed it.

Then the Sui added a softer approach. Wendi freed the former Chen lands from taxes for ten years, and his son Yang Guang, the future Emperor Yangdi, governed the south as viceroy from 591 to 600. Married to a princess from the southern Liang royal family, he ruled fairly mildly and won over southern elites. Click “win southern support” for details.

Why this matters: this is where conquest turns into integration. As the gold box says, reunification did not mean the south was treated as an equal partner, but force alone was not enough to hold it. You will meet Yang Guang again as Yangdi on slide 17.

Check yourself: Why do you think the Sui combined tax relief and mild rule with force after the 590 revolt?

Act II · The reunited empire

Building the Machine

The Sui learned to move officials, grain, taxes, workers, soldiers—and belief.

AI-generated historical interpretation · Dunhuang-inspired mural style

Act II shifts from conquest to the machinery of rule. The AI-generated image shows canal construction and grain barges in the same frame. That combination captures the double meaning of Sui state-building: the canal was a remarkable tool for feeding capitals and moving supplies, and it was also built through enormous compulsory labor drafts.

The “machine” in the title is not a literal machine. It is the linked system of officials, registers, waterways, taxes, labor obligations, military service, law, and religious claims that allowed one court to govern a reunited empire. Each part solved a real problem. Court appointments reduced the power of local families. Canals connected southern grain to northern capitals. Registers showed the state who owed taxes or service. Buddhist patronage gave Wendi’s rule a moral language that could cross regional divisions.

As you move through this act, notice that every tool of integration can also become a tool of extraction. That tension prepares the tragedy’s final act.

Check yourself: Why is the canal both an achievement and a warning?

Problem 1 · who governs?

The court began taking appointments away from powerful local families.

Before the Sui: local elites ranked candidates through the Nine Rank System.
Under Wendi: the court appointed prefecture and county officials.
From 587: prefectures sent candidates to the capital for written testing.
Under Yangdi: the jinshi examination appeared around 605–607.
This was the beginning of a shift—not yet the mature examination system.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

This timeline follows one big change: who decided which men became government officials.

Before the Sui, the Nine Rank System let local elites rank candidates for office, so powerful families largely controlled who got government posts. Under Wendi, the Sui ended that system, and the court began appointing prefecture and county officials itself. (A prefecture is a local district.) From 587, each prefecture sent three candidates a year to the capital, where written tests helped decide who would serve. Around 605–607, Yangdi added the “presented scholar” (jinshi) exam; historians debate the exact date.

Why this matters: this is integration in action. By controlling appointments, the court tied local government to the center instead of to local families. But read the gold box carefully: the Sui began the shift toward exams; it did not create the full exam system. Under the Tang, schools and exams grew, and the mature system took centuries to develop.

Check yourself: How did replacing the Nine Rank System with court appointments shift power between local families and the emperor?

The Sui began a shift toward written examinations; the mature system developed later.

Open the video on YouTube

This video connects the Sui beginnings of written examinations to the much longer history of China’s civil-service examination system. It is your instructor Steven Austin’s video, China’s Examination Hell. The later examination world described in the video became larger, more competitive, and more culturally important than the small Sui system you have just studied.

Keep the chronology straight. The Sui did not suddenly create the complete examination system. Wendi ended the Nine Rank System and brought local appointments more directly under court control. From 587, prefectures sent candidates to the capital for written testing. Yangdi later added the jinshi, or “presented scholar,” category. Under the Tang and later dynasties, schools, examinations, and examination culture expanded.

As you watch, record three short notes: what successful candidates were expected to know, how examinations could widen recruitment, and why access remained unequal. These notes will help you distinguish the ideal of selection by learning from the social advantages that shaped who could compete.

Infrastructure and integration

The Grand Canal moved southern grain toward northern power centers.

  • Linked the Yellow River and Yangzi River systems.
  • Wendi dug the first sections in the 580s; most was dug under Yangdi, 605–610, reusing older rivers and canals.
  • Reached the Beijing area (608) and Hangzhou (610).
  • Built with forced labor: the Book of Sui reports over a million workers for single sections.

The Sui canal routes, 584–610

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; Book of Sui (Suishu), ch. 3.

×

The Sui canal routes, 584–610

  • 584, Wendi: the Guangtong Canal links the capital, Chang’an, to the Yellow River, following an old Han-dynasty canal.
  • 587, Wendi: the Shanyang Canal links the Huai River to the Yangzi, reopening a canal first dug in the 400s BCE.
  • 605, Yangdi: the Tongji Canal links Luoyang to the Huai River. The Book of Sui says over a million men and women were drafted to dig it.
  • 608, Yangdi: the Yongji Canal runs north to Zhuo commandery, near modern Beijing, again with over a million workers.
  • 610, Yangdi: the Jiangnan Canal is rebuilt south of the Yangzi to Yuhang (modern Hangzhou).

Much of the system followed older rivers and canals, but it was still a huge project built with forced labor. In the late 1200s, the Yuan dynasty cut a shorter route through Shandong to its capital at modern Beijing.

The Grand Canal is one of the Sui’s most famous achievements, and this map shows why.

Read the map: the Sui capitals, Chang’an and Luoyang, sit in the northwest near the Yellow River (labeled Huang He). China’s richest farmland lay far to the southeast, around the Yangzi. The double lines are canals linking those river systems. Follow them north to the Beijing area (608) and south to Hangzhou (610). The map also shows some later Tang branches, so not every line is Sui.

Wendi dug the first sections in the 580s, but most of the system was built under Yangdi between 605 and 610, largely by linking and reusing older rivers and canals. Click “The Sui canal routes, 584–610” to see each section.

Why this matters: moving heavy loads of grain by water was much easier than hauling them overland, so the canal helped feed the capitals and armies and made a unified empire easier to govern. That is integration. But the Book of Sui says over a million men and women were drafted to dig single sections, a cost that points ahead to overreach. The Tang kept using the canal, as slide 17 shows.

Check yourself: Why would capitals in the northwest depend on a canal reaching the south?

Problem 3 · what does each household owe?

Once a family entered the register, the state could reach its land, labor, and sons.

1Count the household
2Assign land
3Collect grain and cloth
4Demand labor or military service
609 register: 8,907,546 households · 46,019,956 people
Registration made the empire governable. It also made overmobilization possible.

Sources: Book of Sui (Suishu), ch. 29; Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty.”

This slide explains how the Sui “saw” its people: by writing them down.

The big number comes from the official household register of 609, preserved in the Book of Sui: 8,907,546 households and 46,019,956 people. Treat these as registered figures, not a full count. People who fled, hid, or were never recorded do not appear, so neither number captures everyone living in China.

The registers mattered because the state’s other systems depended on them. Under the equal-field system, the state assigned farmland to households in return for taxes and labor. Under the fubing system, farmers served as soldiers in turns, in the capital or on the frontier, in exchange for land. Grain and cloth taxes paid for the government. The Sui and Tang both kept modified versions of these systems from earlier northern dynasties.

Why this matters: a register is a tool of integration: it lets the court see and count people, land, taxes, and soldiers. But the same tool made it possible to draft those people again and again, which is where overreach begins.

Check yourself: Why would a government that wants taxes and soldiers care so much about counting households?

Problem 4 · why should the conquered accept Sui rule?

A usurper presented himself as the Buddhist protector of “all the people.”

581: Wendi restored Buddhism after Northern Zhou’s ban.
Cakravartin: he claimed the role of an ideal Buddhist protector-king.
601: relics traveled to temples across the empire in imitation of Ashoka.
Religion gave a violent seizure of power a language of universal moral purpose.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

This slide shows a quieter tool of power: religion.

Wendi and his empress were committed Buddhists. The Northern Zhou had banned Buddhism in 574, and in 581, the year he founded the Sui, Wendi began restoring it. He presented himself as a cakravartin, an ideal Buddhist king who uses his power to protect the faith. In 601, he sent Buddha relics to temples across the empire, copying Ashoka, the Indian king famous for spreading Buddhism. At the same time, he revived Confucian court rituals, so he drew on more than one tradition. In Chapter 4 you saw earlier rulers support Buddhism too; Wendi built on that pattern.

Why this matters: Wendi had seized the throne by force, so he needed ways to show he had the right to rule. Buddhism gave him the image of a protector of the faith and of all his subjects, and the relic campaign reached temples across the newly reunited realm. That is integration through shared belief. But keep the order of events straight, as the gold box says: Buddhism supported Sui rule; it did not win the reunification. The armies did that.

Check yourself: What is a cakravartin, and how did Wendi’s 601 relic campaign fit that model?

Primary source · Wendi’s relic edict, 601

What did Wendi promise his subjects?

Read closely, on your own:

  1. According to Wendi, who can reach enlightenment?
  2. Why might an emperor who seized the throne in 581 want to be seen as protecting the spiritual welfare of “all the people”?

Four seas: the whole known world, meaning everyone under the emperor. Karma: the good or bad results of a person’s actions, in this life and future lives.

This is a primary source: words from the time, not a modern summary. It comes from Wendi’s 601 edict sending Buddha relics to temples across the empire, as translated in the course textbook.

How to read it: start with who is included. “All the people within the four seas” means everyone in the known world, that is, everyone under the emperor, and “without exception” drives the point home. Then look at what is promised: good karma (the good results of good actions), happy future lives, and in the end enlightenment for “one and all.” Notice the “us” in the last line: the emperor counts himself among those being carried toward enlightenment.

Why this matters: an edict is also political. Wendi seized the throne in 581 and killed rivals to keep it. Presenting himself as the ruler who cares for the spiritual welfare of all his subjects gave his power a moral purpose beyond force, and the message reached every part of the empire, north and south. Try the two questions on the slide before you read on.

Check yourself: Find one word or phrase in the edict that stresses that everyone is included. Why might Wendi stress that point in an empire that had only recently been reunited?

Yangdi’s imperial barge and canal laborers

Act III · 604–618

Breaking the Empire

Every triumph required another draft, another convoy, another household sacrifice.

AI-generated historical interpretation · Dunhuang-inspired mural style

Act III begins with the same state machinery at a much higher speed. The AI-generated image shows Emperor Yangdi aboard an imperial barge while laborers strain on the towpath. The image is not a record of one documented journey; it combines court magnificence, canal transport, and compulsory labor to make the act’s central contrast visible.

Yangdi inherited a reunified realm, registered households, appointed officials, canals, armies, and an ambitious vision of imperial power. He used them to build Luoyang, extend the canal network, repair frontier defenses, stage grand tours, and launch repeated campaigns. Some projects produced lasting benefits. The canal in particular remained essential under the Tang. But each project drew workers, soldiers, grain, animals, carts, and cloth from the same communities.

The question is no longer whether the Sui state can mobilize the empire. It plainly can. The issue is whether it can recognize when further mobilization threatens the society on which the state depends.

Check yourself: What does the contrast between the barge and the towpath represent?

The tragic protagonist · Yangdi, ruled 604–618

Yangdi magnified both the power and the cost of the Sui state.

  • 604: takes the throne when his father dies.
  • 605: begins a second capital at Luoyang and the canal network (605–610).
  • 607–608: drafts huge labor gangs to rebuild the Great Wall.
  • 612–614: launches costly, failed wars against Goguryeo.
Histories written under the Tang painted Yangdi as a cruel, wasteful tyrant. Historians now see that picture as partly the product of a hostile record, though his projects and wars did cause great suffering.

Source: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty.”

This slide asks you to judge Yangdi for yourself.

Start with the timeline. In 604, Yang Guang, the prince who had governed the south, took the throne as Yangdi. In 605 he began a second capital at Luoyang and the canal network (605–610). In 607–608 he drafted huge labor gangs to rebuild the Great Wall, and in 612–614 he launched costly, failed wars against Goguryeo in Korea.

Look at the portrait. Like Wendi’s on slide 5, it comes from the Thirteen Emperors scroll attributed to Yan Liben. It is an idealized image painted under the Tang, not a likeness from life.

Read the record critically. Histories written under the Tang painted Yangdi as a cruel, wasteful tyrant, the classic “bad last emperor.” The Tang had reason to make the dynasty it replaced look unfit to rule, so historians today treat that picture as partly the product of a hostile record. Still, his projects and wars really did cause great suffering. The Tang writer Pi Rixiu captured both sides: the canal harmed the people of the Sui, but the people of the Tang could not count its benefits.

Check yourself: Was Yangdi more a builder or a tyrant? What is one piece of evidence for each side, and which side do you find stronger?

Imperial ambitions

Both Sui emperors treated the empire’s frontiers as unfinished.

South

Wendi retook the Hanoi region in 602. In 605, Yangdi’s army pushed on into Champa, in central Vietnam.

Northeast

Both emperors attacked Goguryeo, a Korean kingdom that reached into southern Manchuria. It never fell to the Sui.

Sui rulers measured their empire against the lands once held by the earlier Han dynasty.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

This slide zooms out to the edges of the empire.

Read the map. It comes from a 1935 historical atlas by Albert Herrmann, so it uses old spellings. The yellow line traces the Sui borders. At the top right, beyond the northeast border, find Kokurye, today spelled Goguryeo. At the bottom left, find Chiao-chih (Jiaozhi), the region around modern Hanoi.

Both Sui emperors saw the empire as unfinished, because parts of modern Korea and Vietnam had once been ruled by the Han dynasty, the great empire the Sui measured itself against. In the south, Wendi retook the Hanoi region in 602, and in 605 Yangdi’s army pushed on into Champa, in central Vietnam. In the northeast, both emperors attacked Goguryeo, a Korean kingdom that reached into southern Manchuria. It never fell to the Sui.

Why this matters: expansion was not one policy with one result. The next two slides show a costly partial success in the south and a disaster in the northeast. Notice how far both frontiers lie from the capitals, and imagine moving an army and its food that far.

Check yourself: Why did Sui rulers think of parts of Korea and Vietnam as lands they ought to control?

Gamble 1 · Champa, 605

The Sui defeated the elephants—and lost men to distance, climate, and disease.

602: Wendi’s forces recovered the Hanoi region.
605: Liu Fang pushed farther south into Champa.
Battle: Sui troops trapped charging elephants in hidden pits.
Afterward: disease ravaged the army; Liu Fang died on the return march.
A battlefield victory can still be a strategic disaster.

Sources: Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty”; course textbook, ch. 5.

This timeline shows that winning battles is not the same as winning a war you can afford.

In 602, under Wendi, Sui forces retook the Hanoi region from a local ruler. In 605, under Yangdi, General Liu Fang pushed farther south into Champa, a kingdom in what is now central Vietnam. Champa’s army used war elephants. Sui troops pretended to retreat and dug hidden pits to trap the elephants, and they won the battle.

But the environment turned against them. Soldiers from the north had little resistance to tropical diseases such as malaria, and disease ravaged the army. Liu Fang himself fell sick and died on the way home.

Why this matters: read the gold box. A distant campaign can weaken an army even when it wins, because supply lines, climate, and disease can cost more than enemy soldiers do. This is an early sign of overreach: each campaign drew soldiers and supplies from home, and the costs added up.

Check yourself: The Sui beat Champa’s elephants. Why can the Champa campaign still be seen as a costly failure?

Gamble 2 · Goguryeo, 612

At the Salsu River, imperial scale became imperial catastrophe.

Mass mobilization: the Book of Sui claims 1,133,800 combat troops, plus even more carriers.
Stalled advance: Liaodong’s forts held; supplies ran short.
Salsu retreat: Goguryeo forces shattered the army sent toward Pyongyang.
Traditional figures: 305,000 marched in; 2,700 returned. The totals may be inflated, but the disaster was real.

Open the campaign map and source caution

Sources: Book of Sui (Suishu), ch. 4; Britannica, “China: The Sui dynasty.”

×

The Salsu River disaster, 612

The Book of Sui says Yangdi gathered 1,133,800 combat troops for the 612 campaign, with twice as many people carrying supplies.

When the sieges of Goguryeo’s forts in Liaodong stalled, a force said to number 305,000 marched on the capital, Pyongyang. Short of food and worn out, it turned back. The Goguryeo general Ŭlchi Mundŏk attacked it at the Salsu River (today’s Chongchon River). The histories say only 2,700 men made it home.

These are traditional figures from histories written after the Sui fell. Historians think some totals were inflated, but the losses were clearly enormous.

This timeline shows the Sui’s biggest military failure. Goguryeo, a strong Korean kingdom with its capital near modern Pyongyang and lands reaching into southern Manchuria, resisted four Sui campaigns.

Wendi’s attack in 598 failed because of supply problems and storms. In 612, Yangdi’s armies could not take the forts of Liaodong, and a force sent toward Pyongyang was destroyed at the Salsu River. Click the river name for a map and the story. In 613, Yangdi called off a new campaign when the aristocrat Yang Xuangan rebelled inside China. In 614, Goguryeo asked for peace, but the Sui gained no lasting control.

Read the numbers carefully. The traditional figures say 305,000 men marched toward Pyongyang and only 2,700 came back, and the Book of Sui counts 1,133,800 combat troops for 612. Historians think some of these totals were probably inflated, partly because they come from histories written after the Sui fell, under a dynasty with reason to make Yangdi’s wars look as disastrous as possible. Focus on the enormous scale and the repeated burden rather than the exact numbers.

Check yourself: Besides enemy soldiers, what were two reasons the Goguryeo campaigns failed?

The bill comes due

One household could be asked to finance the dynasty’s entire vision.

IGraintaxes and campaign supplies
IIClothregular taxes and military needs
IIILaborcanals, walls, roads, and capitals
IVSoldiersfrontier service and distant invasions
State capacity
count and mobilize
→
Repeated demands
the same households again
→
Refusal
flight, desertion, rebellion
The state’s strength became dangerous when households had no reserve left for the next demand—or the next disaster.

This slide explains the mechanism behind the Sui collapse. Read the three boxes as a chain of cause and effect.

Imperial aims, such as extending the frontiers and recovering lands once held by the Han, required mobilization: drafting soldiers and workers and moving food and equipment. A campaign like the one against Goguryeo needed not just fighters but ships, carts, grain, clothing, armor, and people to carry supplies. The Book of Sui says the supply carriers for 612 numbered twice the combat troops. All of that came from the same registered households, and the result was household strain: labor and resources pulled away from local communities.

Why this matters: the two cards show the paradox of a strong state. What the Sui could do (build canals, move armies, and organize supplies over long distances) was impressive. What that demanded (repeated drafts and transport duties) left families less able to absorb shocks like a flood or a failed harvest. This is overreach in its clearest form, and you will see its results on slide 23.

Check yourself: In two or three sentences, how could a war far away in Korea make life harder for a farming family in north China?

The people answer · Shandong, 611

When obedience looked like death, rebellion began to look rational.

Draft: men were being summoned for war in Liaodong.
Choice: risk death far from home—or fight the state at home.
Wang Bo: one of the first rebel leaders to turn that fear into a cause.
The government could still issue orders. It could no longer make obedience seem safer than resistance.

This AI-generated scene introduces rebellion from below. It imagines drafted farmers and deserters gathering on high ground while government troops approach through the valley. The abandoned tools and fields connect rebellion to the household burdens you have already studied. The image is interpretive; it does not claim to portray Wang Bo or a precisely documented location.

In 611, before the disastrous 612 invasion, Yangdi’s government was already drafting men and supplies for war against Goguryeo. Wang Bo led one of the first important revolts from Changbai Mountain in Shandong. This is not the better-known Changbai Mountain on the modern China–Korea border. Rebels could present themselves as an alternative to a state that appeared to offer drafted men only hardship and death far from home.

The next slide preserves a song traditionally attributed to Wang Bo. Read it as political persuasion. It turns the government’s threat—death for rebellion—into an argument for rebellion: if obedience also means death, fear loses its power.

Check yourself: Why could military conscription make a rebel leader seem less dangerous than the government?

Primary source · a rebel song, 611

“Don’t go to Liaodong to die for nothing.”

The song’s argument

Government service and rebellion both threaten death. Rebellion at least offers agency, comrades, and a chance to remain near home.

What changed

Fear no longer protected the dynasty once subjects believed obedience was equally dangerous.

This primary source lets you hear from the people who were being drafted, not just from emperors and officials.

The context: in 611, Yangdi was drafting men for his war against Goguryeo in Liaodong (southern Manchuria). A man named Wang Bo led one of the first revolts, from Changbai Mountain in Shandong. That is a different mountain from the Changbai Mountain on today’s border with Korea. The song is traditionally credited to him, but we can’t be sure he wrote it. The translation is adapted from the Chinese text in a collection of Sui poetry.

How to read it: the first eight lines paint the rebel as a hero, dressed in red silk, armed with a spear that “stabs halfway to the sky,” eating well on the mountain, and charging when government troops arrive. Then the last two lines switch to “I” and make the argument: if drafted men will die in Liaodong anyway, they lose nothing by rebelling at home.

Why this matters: the song shows overmobilization from below. When the draft felt like a death sentence, rebellion started to look like the better choice.

Check yourself: Why does the singer think rebelling is no worse than obeying the draft, and what does that suggest about how ordinary people saw the Goguryeo war?

The empire fractures · 613–617

The Sui lost cooperation from below—and command from above.

Communities break

  • Floods, droughts, and epidemics
  • Labor and supply demands
  • Deserters join armed bands

Elites defect

  • Yang Xuangan rebels in 613
  • Governors and generals raise armies
  • Li Yuan takes Chang’an in 617
A dynasty cannot survive when households stop supplying it, soldiers stop obeying it, and officials begin replacing it.

By the mid-610s, several pressures were reinforcing one another. Floods, droughts, and epidemics disrupted harvests and travel. Labor and military drafts removed people and supplies from communities that needed them. Deserters and hungry families joined armed groups. Those groups then made transport, taxation, and local government harder, weakening the state’s ability to respond to the original crises.

The collapse was not simply a peasant revolt. In 613, Yang Xuangan—an aristocrat and son of the powerful minister Yang Su—rebelled while Yangdi was campaigning against Goguryeo. Governors, commanders, and court officials increasingly acted for themselves. Li Yuan was one of those insiders: a Sui governor with family and marriage ties to the northern ruling elite.

This matters because states depend on cooperation at several levels. The Sui lost the labor of households, the obedience of soldiers, and finally the loyalty of elites who commanded armies and provinces. When those layers failed together, the central court could no longer restore order.

Check yourself: Why is it misleading to describe the Sui collapse as only a peasant uprising?

The final scene · Jiangdu, 618

The guards enter. The dynasty ends. The state remains.

Spring 618: officers associated with Yuwen Huaji kill Yangdi at Jiangdu.
Meanwhile: Li Yuan rules Chang’an through a Sui puppet emperor.
Summer 618: Li Yuan removes the puppet and proclaims the Tang.
The Sui royal house fell. Its capitals, canals, laws, offices, and reunified realm passed to new rulers.

This slide returns to the cold open, now with the causes in view. By 618, Yangdi was at Jiangdu in the south. He had withdrawn from the northern political center while rebel armies and former Sui officials competed for territory. Officers led by members of Yuwen Huaji’s group killed him in spring 618. The AI-generated image imagines the isolation and betrayal of the final night without depicting the murder itself.

At the same time, Li Yuan controlled Chang’an. He had entered the capital in late 617, installed Yangdi’s grandson as a puppet Sui emperor, and presented himself as restoring order. After Yangdi died, Li Yuan removed the puppet and declared the Tang dynasty. That sequence shows how carefully a successful rebel could use the forms of the old dynasty before replacing it.

The tragedy is now complete: the institutions that allowed the Sui to mobilize the empire could not force continued loyalty after rulers exhausted the people and divided the elite.

Check yourself: How did Li Yuan use Sui legitimacy before claiming the throne for himself?

The Tang inherits the Sui state

Tang founders emerged from the Sui’s northwestern military world.

  • Li Yuan / Gaozu was a Sui governor who became the first Tang emperor in 618.
  • Li Shimin / Taizong was his son and a successful commander.
  • The Tang ruling family belonged to the same northwestern military aristocracy as the Sui and was related to the Sui royal family by marriage.
The Tang replaced the Sui dynasty while inheriting its unified territory and many of its institutions.

Sources: Britannica, “China” (Sui and early Tang sections); course textbook, ch. 5; Penn Museum, object C395.

This slide introduces the family that replaced the Sui, and it came from the same world.

Li Yuan, known as Gaozu after he became emperor, was a Sui governor based at Taiyuan who founded the Tang in 618. His son Li Shimin, later Emperor Taizong, was a skilled commander. The Li family belonged to the same northwestern military aristocracy as the Sui and was related to the Sui royal family by marriage. Histories written under Taizong overstated Li Shimin’s role in the founding, so read those accounts with care.

Look at the relief. This stone carving comes from Taizong’s tomb, not from the Sui; it was made in 636–649. It shows Saluzi (“Autumn Dew”), one of six warhorses carved for the tomb, with General Qiu Xinggong pulling an arrow from its chest after a battle near Luoyang in 621. Notice the saddle, the armor, and the quiver: the carving celebrates a ruling family that won power on horseback. The original is in the Penn Museum in Philadelphia.

Why this matters: the Tang was a new dynasty, but not a new ruling class.

Check yourself: What does this relief suggest about how the Tang founders wanted to be remembered?

Why the Sui mattered

What the Tang inherited from the Sui

Law

The Kaihuang Code of 583 became the model for the Tang Code.

Central government

Three central ministries, with boards under them; the early Tang kept this structure.

Local government

In 583 the Sui cut a whole layer of local government (the commanderies); the court appointed local officials.

Capital

Daxing, the new capital Wendi built in the 580s, became the Tang capital, Chang’an.

Grand Canal

Yangdi’s canals kept carrying southern grain north for the Tang.

Exams

Sui beginnings of written exams grew into a larger Tang system.

The Sui lasted only 37 years, but the Tang built a dynasty of nearly 300 years on Sui foundations.

Sources: Britannica, “China” (Sui and early Tang sections); Book of Sui (Suishu), ch. 29.

This slide answers the second learning objective: what the Tang inherited from the Sui. Use it as a checklist.

Law: the Kaihuang Code of 583 became the model for the Tang Code. Central government: the early Tang kept the Sui structure of three central ministries. Local government: in 583 the Sui cut out a whole layer of local government, the commanderies, and the court appointed local officials; the Tang kept that pattern of court control. Capital: Daxing, the capital Wendi built in the 580s, became the Tang capital, Chang’an. Grand Canal: it kept carrying southern grain north. Exams: the Sui beginnings grew into a larger Tang system.

Why this matters: the Sui lasted only 37 years (581–618), but the Tang ruled for nearly 300 years on Sui foundations. So the Sui was not simply a failure. Its conquest and integration succeeded and lasted; what failed was its overreach. That is why historians often discuss the two dynasties together as the “Sui–Tang” era.

Check yourself: Cover the slide and list as many of the six inheritances as you can. Which one do you think mattered most to the Tang, and why?

Epilogue

The dynasty died. Its state survived.

What collapsed

The Sui royal house, Yangdi’s authority, and obedience to the dynasty.

What endured

Reunification, capitals, canals, law, ministries, registration, and early examinations.

Who inherited it

Li Yuan and the Tang—insiders from the same northwestern military world.

The Sui tragedy: Wendi built a powerful imperial machine. Yangdi drove it past the breaking point. The Tang learned to operate what remained.

This is the final interpretation of the lecture. The dynasty died, but much of its state survived. The Tang inherited a reunified territorial core, the capital at Daxing—renamed Chang’an—the Grand Canal, the Kaihuang law code as a model, central ministries, a simplified system of local government, household registration, and the beginnings of court-controlled written examinations.

That survival changes how we judge the Sui. A dynasty that lasted only thirty-seven years might look like a simple failure. Yet the Tang built one of China’s most famous empires on Sui foundations. What failed was not the goal of reunification or every Sui institution. What failed was the political control needed to keep mobilization within sustainable limits.

The tragedy therefore has an irony: Yangdi’s projects helped destroy his dynasty, but some—especially the canals—continued to benefit later rulers. The people of the Sui bore the immediate costs; the Tang inherited many of the long-term gains.

Check yourself: Complete this sentence with two examples: “The Sui dynasty died, but the Sui state survived through…”

Narrative review

Retell the tragedy in nine terms

Wendi · Yangdi

First and second Sui emperors (ruled 581–604 and 604–618).

Xianbei

Nomadic peoples from the northern grasslands whose leaders ruled much of north China.

Nine Rank System

Older way of choosing officials through local elites; ended by the Sui.

Grand Canal

Waterway linking the Yellow and Yangzi river systems.

Equal-field system

The state assigned farmland to households in return for taxes and labor.

Fubing

Farmers who served as soldiers in turns, in exchange for land.

Cakravartin

Ideal Buddhist king who uses his power to protect the faith.

Mobilization

Drafting soldiers and workers and moving food and equipment for war or building.

Goguryeo

Korean kingdom that defeated repeated Sui invasions.

Next: how early Tang rulers strengthened and extended the Sui state.

Use this slide for your final review. Try this: cover the definitions, explain each term in your own words, and then check yourself against the slide.

Don’t just memorize definitions. Try using the terms to retell the lecture’s story in order. Wendi, whose family may have had Xianbei roots, founded the Sui and reunited China. The Sui ended the Nine Rank System, counted households for the equal-field system and the fubing farmer-soldiers, built the first sections of the Grand Canal, and presented Wendi as a cakravartin. Under Yangdi, mobilization for canals and for wars against Goguryeo pushed households too far.

Study tip: sort the nine terms under the lecture’s three headings: conquest, integration, and overreach. Some terms fit more than one. The Grand Canal, for example, held the empire together but was built with forced labor. Being able to explain why a term fits two headings is a good sign you understand it.

In the next lecture, you will see how early Tang rulers strengthened and extended the Sui state.

Check yourself: Which two terms on this slide best explain the Sui collapse, and how are they connected?

Five-minute individual writing

Write the Sui dynasty’s obituary.

In about 100 words, explain what the Sui achieved, the fatal mistake that destroyed it, and what survived under the Tang.

AchievementName the Sui’s greatest success.
Fatal mistakeIdentify the choice or pattern that made collapse likely.
EvidenceUse two specific events, people, dates, or sources.
LegacyExplain what the Tang inherited.

Write from memory first. Use the deck only to correct names and dates after your argument is on the page.

This activity asks you to turn the lecture’s evidence into a short historical judgment. An obituary records a death, identifies what the subject accomplished, and explains what ended it. Your obituary should do all three for the Sui dynasty.

Begin with one sentence stating the Sui’s greatest achievement. You might choose political reunification, the conquest of the south, the Grand Canal, court control over appointments, or another institution inherited by the Tang. Then identify the fatal mistake. Strong choices include repeated mobilization for construction and war, failure to stop after the 612 disaster, or the loss of cooperation from both households and elites. Support each judgment with one concrete piece of evidence—a date, event, person, institution, or primary source from the lecture.

End with the historical irony: the dynasty fell, but the Tang kept important parts of the state it had built. Write from memory first, then use the deck to correct names or dates.

Check yourself: Does your obituary include an achievement, a fatal mistake, two specific pieces of evidence, and a surviving legacy?
